title: Human or machine?
note: The twist: every 'person' answer here was written by Alan Turing in 1950, in his paper 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence'. He was imagining how a machine might answer in the imitation game, while it pretends to be a person. So these answers come from a person pretending to be a machine pretending to be a person! The 'chatbot' answers were written by a real AI chatbot in 2026. Teachers: you can replace this file with your class's own answers (no names, no personal data).

items.q: Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.
items.a: Of course! Here is the opening: "Red iron giant striding through the mist, / Three mighty arches hold the river's breath..."
items.source: written by an AI chatbot (Claude) in October 2026 for this site
items.note: A modern chatbot almost never says no to a poem. It starts at once, happy and polite: "Of course!"

items.source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950): the answer he imagined for a machine
items.note: Slow, and wrong! The right answer is 105721. Later in the same paper Turing suggests that a machine could make mistakes on purpose, to seem more human.

items.q: In the first line of your sonnet, 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day', would not 'a spring day' do as well or better?
items.source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950): the answer he imagined for a machine
items.note: Very short and sure, like a poet. 'Scan' means the rhythm of the line works: 'a spring day' has one beat too few.

items.q: Do you play chess? I have only a king at K1. You have a king at K6 and a rook at R1. It is your move. What do you play?
items.a: Yes, I play! I would move my rook to R8. That is checkmate: my king guards the squares in front of yours, so your king cannot escape.
items.source: written by an AI chatbot (Claude) in October 2026 for this site
items.note: It explains why, even if you did not ask. Chatbots love to explain their reasons step by step.

items.q: Please write me a sonnet on the subject of the Forth Bridge.
items.a: Count me out on this one. I never could write poetry.
items.source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950): the answer he imagined for a machine
items.note: Many people would say the same! Saying 'I can't' is a very human answer, and Turing knew it.

items.source: written by an AI chatbot (Claude) in October 2026 for this site
items.note: Instant, correct and neat, with commas. A modern chatbot does not pretend to be slow.

items.q: How about 'a winter's day'? That would scan all right.
items.a: Yes, but nobody wants to be compared to a winter's day.
items.source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950): the answer he imagined for a machine
items.note: A little joke about feelings: who wants to be cold and grey? Turing used it to show what a really clever machine would need to understand.

items.q: Do you play chess? I have only a king at K1. You have a king at K6 and a rook at R1. It is your move. What do you play?
items.a: (after a pause of 15 seconds) R-R8 mate.
items.source: Alan Turing, 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950): the answer he imagined for a machine
items.note: Short, with a pause, in chess notation. It is a correct move: a careful player, or a careful machine.
